insights.text: Your body is the temple. What was kept in the innermost room was the law. So when Jeremiah says the law is written on the inward parts, the tablets are back where they belong. The deepest place in a man holds a standard, not a feeling.
insights.blip: The manna and the rod sat there too — provision and priesthood. Fed, led, and governed, all behind the veil.

insights.text: Yahuah's presence sat in one room, behind one veil, and one man went in once a year. Joel wasn't promising a revival. He was promising a new temple — the Spirit poured out on all flesh, so the innermost room is now a person. Shavuot was the day it started.

Prince of this world. Prince of Peace. Two princes named in the Book, and neither one holds a deed — the earth is Yahuah's, and the fulness thereof. Allegiance shows up in the statutes a man keeps. Whose are you keeping?

The ten virgins is not a story about being late, and it is not a story about how much of the Spirit anyone had. It is about a priesthood, a light, and what happens to a house when that light goes out. The commandment is a lamp and the Torah is light. Nobody sells the Spirit of Yahuah, and verse nine sends them out to buy.

Yahushua said in my Father's house are many mansions, and it gets read as real estate waiting in the sky. The word is not a mansion, it is a dwelling place, and He uses it again a few verses later: we will come to him and make our dwelling with him. The house was never a subdivision. It was people.

Isaiah gets read like a drawer of loose verses — a Christmas line here, a suffering servant there. It runs in four blocks, in order, each covering its own stretch of time. Notice what that does to the last block: not one verse in it has ever been quoted as already fulfilled.

The table has two things on it, and most teaching stops at one. The cup is entry — the blood, the door, the way in. The bread is the walk that follows, and a man who takes the cup and never touches the bread has come through the door and sat down in the entryway.

When they replaced Judas they did not vote on character. They named one requirement: the man had to have been there from the immersion of John to the day Yahushua was taken up, and to have seen Him risen. That is not a job description anyone alive can meet.

A monument of the ten commandments goes up outside a courthouse and the crowd cheers. That same week the sermon says the law was nailed to the cross. One of those two is wrong, and it is not the stone.

Ask what the owner came to collect and the whole reading straightens out. Not grapes, not attendance, not a building. Righteousness in his people, which Moses already defined as keeping the commandments. The renters were removed for failing to grow it. The vineyard stayed exactly where it was.
insights.studyLabel: They Wanted the House Without the Owner

insights.text: The apostles reported the fruit; Yahushua told them what it meant in the unseen world. He was not giving a history lesson — He was watching the enemy's grip on men break in real time, and the tree would finish it.

The disciples asked “when” the temple would fall, and the parable answers “why”: the men handed the law of Yahuah to feed the household buried it in the ground instead, so the charge was taken from them and weighed into hands that would hand it out.

Learn not the way of the heathen. Four empires supplied what the command forbade: Egypt the sun and its day, Babylon the mother and the calendar, Greece the immortal soul and the creed’s vocabulary, Rome the twenty-fifth of December and a day of rest set by statute. Wrap those four in a bow and the name on the package is Christianity.

The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, and Balaam saw that Sceptre as a person rising out of Israel. Yahuah is the King, and Yahushua is the Sceptre He holds out, a sceptre of righteousness, the Father's instrument of rule, not a second throne. That righteousness is given by believing in the Son, and all who believe come under the King's Sceptre.

Everyone has heard of the mark of the beast on the right hand and the forehead, but few notice that Yahuah asked His people to wear only two things in those same places: His Law and His feast. Daniel's little horn would "think to change times and laws," the appointed feasts and the Law, the very two things. The mark is Yahuah's sign with the calendar and the commandments swapped out.

Everyone knows the sun, moon, and stars were given for signs and seasons, but few notice that Yahuah named the moon as the witness to Messiah's throne: "It shall be established for ever as the moon, and as a faithful witness in heaven." Every month the moon renews, she testifies that the throne of Yahushua still stands. A calendar that throws out the moon throws out the witness, and whoever rejects the witness rejects the throne she testifies to.

Modern teaching reads this parable as an altar call, but Scripture settled on the third day of creation that seed brings forth after its kind — so the seed is the law of Yahuah and the fruit is the keeping of it, and the only thing the parable weighs is whether what Yahuah said is still in him at harvest.

Yahushua closed this parable with Joel's sickle, and the field being cut is a man — the seed is Yahuah's own instruction planted in him, the blade and the ear and the full grain are that instruction coming up as his walk, and a pulpit that has declared the law set aside has nothing it can name growing in the middle of the verse.

Whereunto shall we liken the kingdom of Yahuah? Daniel had already answered it — a stone cut out without hands that became a mountain filling the whole earth — so when Yahushua marked the mustard seed as less than all seeds and greater than all herbs, He was supplying the middle Daniel never showed: the kingdom came in the days of those kings, not as a conquest crashing down on Rome, but as a seed put quietly into the ground in a man out of Nazareth.

The parable answers a complaint about fasting nobody was ever commanded to keep, and Yahuah had already named the bottle Himself when He told Jeremiah every bottle would be filled with wine and then said the bottles were the men — so the old bottle is a man hardened around his own traditions until the commandments could not get in, and the new bottle is that same man remade, with the law of Yahuah written on the inside of him.

Ten virgins, five wise and five foolish. What separated them was oil, and Scripture commands oil in a lamp for exactly one purpose — to keep the light in Yahuah's house from going out. The commandment is the lamp and the law is the light, so the five who ran dry were priests who let His instruction die in them.

I will open my mouth in a parable; I will utter dark sayings of old. Yahushua quoted that line about His own teaching, and the word old is the whole point. He was not inventing pictures on the spot — He was using symbols His hearers had carried since childhood, which is why a parable read without the Hebrew Scriptures has nowhere left to go but a moral.

Why speakest thou unto them in parables? His own disciples asked it, and His answer was not that stories make hard truth easy — He said He spoke that way so that some, hearing, would not understand. Every lamp, vineyard, door and seed in them already carried a settled meaning in Torah and the Prophets, and to anyone who had set those Scriptures aside the picture stayed shut.

The talents were never an inventory of a man's abilities — they are the law of Yahuah, the thing He said He would write on a man's heart, weighed into the hands of servants charged to feed the household with it, and the one who buried his talent buried that.

The parable answers a lawyer hunting a loophole in the word neighbour, and the answer is a road with four men on it — one stripped of anything saying whose he is, two holding the altar and the teaching of the law who walked around him, and one shut out of the house who stopped and did for the broken what Yahuah said He would do Himself — because the law had already named the stranger and the enemy, and a neighbour is not settled before a man acts but is what he becomes when he does.
The pulpit teaches you to bind the strong man and take back your goods, but in the parable you are the goods, carried out of the house of bondage the way Israel left Egypt on Pesach night.
